items.title: Elon Musk – "In 36 months, the cheapest place to put AI will be space”
items.summary: Optimus and humanoid manufacturing, Tesla will use 10,000 to 30,000 Optimus robots for self-training, similar to FSD Elon Musk revealed Optimus's new strategy: creating an "Optimus Academy" with 10,000 to 30,000 real robots that will continuously perform various tasks in the real world 24/7, generating massive amounts of real-world data.  Simultaneously, Tesla will use its powerful physics simulation to run millions of virtual robots to accelerate iteration.  Ultimately, this "real-world self-play + large-scale simulation closed-loop" system will enable general artificial intelligence in robots.
items.content:
[Transcript
Elon Musk

Are there really three hours of questions? Are you fucking serious?

Dwarkesh Patel

You don’t think there’s a lot to talk about, Elon?

Elon Musk

Holy fuck man.

John Collison

It’s the most interesting point. All the storylines are converging right now. We’ll see how much we can get through.

Elon Musk

It’s almost like I planned it.

John Collison

Exactly. We’ll get to that.

Elon Musk

But I would never do such a thing…

Orbital data centers
Dwarkesh Patel

As you know better than anybody else, only 10-15% of the total cost of ownership of a data center is energy. That’s the part you’re presumably saving by moving this into space. Most of it’s the GPUs. If they’re in space, it’s harder to service them or you can’t service them. So the depreciation cycle goes down on them. It’s just way more expensive to have the GPUs in space, presumably. What’s the reason to put them in space?

Elon Musk

The availability of energy is the issue. If you look at electrical output outside of China, everywhere outside of China, it’s more or less flat. It’s maybe a slight increase, but pretty close flat. China has a rapid increase in electrical output. But if you’re putting data centers anywhere except China, where are you going to get your electricity? Especially as you scale.

The output of chips is growing pretty much exponentially, but the output of electricity is flat. So how are you going to turn the chips on? Magical power sources? Magical electricity fairies?

Dwarkesh Patel

You’re famously a big fan of solar. One terawatt of solar power, with a 25% capacity factor, that’s like four terawatts of solar panels. It’s 1% of the land area of the United States. We’re in the singularity when we’ve got one terawatt of data centers, right? So what are you running out of exactly?

Elon Musk

How far into the singularity are you though?

Dwarkesh Patel

You tell me.

Elon Musk

Exactly. So I think we’ll find we’re in the singularity and it’ll be like, “Okay, we’ve still got a long way to go.”

Dwarkesh Patel

But is the plan to put it in space after we’ve covered Nevada in solar panels?

Elon Musk

I think it’s pretty hard to cover Nevada in solar panels. You have to get permits. Try getting the permits for that. See what happens.

Dwarkesh Patel

So space is really a regulatory play. It’s harder to build on land than it is in space.

Elon Musk

It’s harder to scale on the ground than it is to scale in space. You’re also going to get about five times the effectiveness of solar panels in space versus the ground, and you don’t need batteries. I almost wore my other shirt, which says, “it’s always sunny in space”. Which it is because you don’t have a day-night cycle, seasonality, clouds, or an atmosphere in space. The atmosphere alone results in about a 30% loss of energy.

So any given solar panel can do about five times more power in space than on the ground. You also avoid the cost of having batteries to carry you through the night. It’s actually much cheaper to do in space. My prediction is that it will be by far the cheapest place to put AI. It will be space in 36 months or less. Maybe 30 months.

Dwarkesh Patel

36 months?

Elon Musk

Less than 36 months.

Dwarkesh Patel

How do you service GPUs as they fail, which happens quite often in training?

Elon Musk

Actually, it depends on how recent the GPUs are that have arrived. At this point, we find our GPUs to be quite reliable. There’s infant mortality, which you can obviously iron out on the ground. So you can just run them on the ground and confirm that you don’t have infant mortality with the GPUs.

But once they start working and you’re past the initial debug cycle of Nvidia or whoever’s making the chips—could be Tesla AI6 chips or something like that, or it could be TPUs or Trainiums or whatever—they’re quite reliable past a certain point. So I don’t think the servicing thing is an issue.

But you can mark my words. In 36 months, but probably closer to 30 months, the most economically compelling place to put AI will be space. It will then get ridiculously better to be in space.

The only place you can really scale is space. Once you start thinking in terms of what percentage of the Sun’s power you are harnessing, you realize you have to go to space. You can’t scale very much on Earth.

Dwarkesh Patel

But by very much, to be clear, you’re talking terawatts?

Elon Musk

Yeah. All of the United States currently uses only half a terawatt on average. So if you say a terawatt, that would be twice as much electricity as the United States currently consumes. So that’s quite a lot. Can you imagine building that many data centers, that many power plants?

Those who have lived in software land don’t realize they’re about to have a hard lesson in hardware. It’s actually very difficult to build power plants. You don’t just need power plants, you need all of the electrical equipment. You need the electrical transformers to run the AI transformers.

Now, the utility industry is a very slow industry. They pretty much impedance match to the government, to the Public Utility Commissions. They impedance match literally and figuratively. They’re very slow, because their past has been very slow. So trying to get them to move fast is... Have you ever tried to do an interconnect agreement with a utility at scale, with a lot of power?

Dwarkesh Patel

As a professional podcaster, I can say that I have not, in fact.

John Collison

They need many more views before that becomes an issue.

Elon Musk

They have to do a study for a year. A year later, they’ll come back to you with their interconnect study.

John Collison

Can’t you solve this with your own behind the meter power stuff?

Elon Musk

You can build power plants. That’s what we did at xAI, for Colossus 2.

John Collison

So why talk about the grid? Why not just build GPUs and power co-located?

Elon Musk

That’s what we did.

John Collison

But I’m saying why isn’t this a generalized solution?

Elon Musk

Where do you get the power plants from?

John Collison

When you’re talking about all the issues working with utilities, you can just build private power plants with the data centers.

Elon Musk

Right. But it begs the question of where do you get the power plants from? The power plant makers.

John Collison

Oh, I see what you’re saying. Is this the gas turbine backlog basically?

Elon Musk

Yes. You can drill down to a level further. It’s the vanes and blades in the turbines that are the limiting factor because it’s a very specialized process to cast the blades and vanes in the turbines, assuming you’re using gas power. It’s very difficult to scale other forms of power. You can potentially scale solar, but the tariffs currently for importing solar in the US are gigantic and the domestic solar production is pitiful.

John Collison

Why not make solar? That seems like a good Elon-shaped problem.

Elon Musk

We are going to make solar.

John Collison

Okay.

Elon Musk

Both SpaceX and Tesla are building towards 100 gigawatts a year of solar cell production.

Dwarkesh Patel

How low down the stack? From polysilicon up to the wafer to the final panel?

Elon Musk

I think you’ve got to do the whole thing from raw materials to finish the cell. Now, if it’s going to space, it costs less and it’s easier to make solar cells that go to space because they don’t need much glass.

They don’t need heavy framing because they don’t have to survive weather events. There’s no weather in space. So it’s actually a cheaper solar cell that goes to space than the one on the ground.

Dwarkesh Patel

Is there a path to getting them as cheap as you need in the next 36 months?

Elon Musk

Solar cells are already very cheap. They’re farcically cheap. I think solar cells in China are around $0.25-30/watt or something like that. It’s absurdly cheap. Now put it in space, and it’s five times cheaper. In fact, it’s not five times cheaper, it’s 10 times cheaper because you don’t need any batteries.

So the moment your cost of access to space becomes low, by far the cheapest and most scalable way to generate tokens is space. It’s not even close. It’ll be an order of magnitude easier to scale.

The point is you won’t be able to scale on the ground. You just won’t. People are going to hit the wall big time on power generation. They already are. The number of miracles in series that the xAI team had to accomplish in order to get a gigawatt of power online was crazy.

We had to gang together a whole bunch of turbines. We then had permit issues in Tennessee and had to go across the border to Mississippi, which is fortunately only a few miles away. But we still then had to run the high power lines a few miles and build the power plant in Mississippi. It was very difficult to build that.

People don’t understand how much electricity you actually need at the generation level in order to power a data center. Because the noobs will look at the power consumption of, say a GB300, and multiply that by a thing and then think that’s the amount of power you need.

John Collison

All the cooling and everything.

Elon Musk

Wake up. That’s a total noob, you’ve never done any hardware in your life before. Besides the GB300, you’ve got to power all of the networking hardware. There’s a whole bunch of CPU and storage stuff that’s happening. You’ve got to size for your peak cooling requirements. That means, can you cool even on the worst hour of the worst day of the year?

It gets pretty frigging hot in Memphis. So you’re going to have a 40% increase on your power just for cooling. That’s assuming you don’t want your data center to turn off on hot days and you want to keep going. There’s another multiplicative element on top of that which is, are you assuming that you never have any hiccups in your power generation?

Actually, sometimes we have to take the generators, some of the power, offline in order to service it. Okay, now you add another 20-25% multiplier on that, because you’ve got to assume that you’ve got to take power offline to service it. So our actual estimate: every 110,000 GB300s—inclusive of networking, CPU, storage, cooling, margin for servicing power—is roughly 300 megawatts.

John Collison

Sorry, say that again.

Elon Musk

What you probably need at the generation level to service 330,000 GB 300s—including all of the associated support networking and everything else, and the peak cooling, and to have some power margin reserve—is roughly a gigawatt.

Dwarkesh Patel

Can I ask a very naive question? You’re describing the engineering details of doing this stuff on Earth. But then there’s analogous engineering difficulties of doing it in space. How do you replace infinite bandwidth with orbital lasers, et cetera, et cetera? How do you make it resistant to radiation?

I don’t know the details of the engineering, but fundamentally, what is the reason to think those challenges which have never had to be addressed before will end up being easier than just building more turbines on Earth? There are companies that build turbines on Earth. They can make more turbines, right?

Elon Musk

Again, try doing it and then you’ll see. The turbines are sold out through 2030.

John Collison

Have you guys considered making your own?

Elon Musk

In order to bring enough power online, I think SpaceX and Tesla will probably have to make the turbine blades, the vanes and blades, internally.

John Collison

But just the blades or the turbines?

Elon Musk

The limiting factor... you can get everything except the blades. They call them blades and vanes. You can get that 12 to 18 months before the vanes and blades. The limiting factor is the vanes and blades. There are only three casting companies in the world that make these, and they’re massively backlogged.

John Collison

Is this Siemens, GE, those guys, or is it a sub company?

Elon Musk

No, it’s other companies. Sometimes they have a little bit of casting capability in-house. But I’m just saying you can just call any of the turbine makers and they will tell you. It’s not top secret. It’s probably on the internet right now.

Dwarkesh Patel

If it wasn’t for the tariffs, would Colossus be solar-powered?

Elon Musk

It would be much easier to make it solar powered, yeah. The tariffs are nuts, several hundred percent.

John Collison

Don’t you know some people?

Elon Musk

The president has... we don’t agree on everything and this administration is not the biggest fan of solar. We also need the land, the permits, and everything. So if you try to move very fast, I do think scaling solar on Earth is a good way to go, but you do need some amount of time to find the land, get the permits, get the solar, pair that with the batteries.

John Collison

Why would it not work to stand up your own solar production? You’re right that you eventually run out of land, but there’s a lot of land here in Texas. There’s a lot of land in Nevada, including private land. It’s not all publicly-owned land. So you’d be able to at least get the next Colossus and the next one after that. At a certain point, you hit a wall. But wouldn’t that work for the moment?

Elon Musk

As I said, we are scaling solar production. There’s a rate at which you can scale physical production of solar cells. We’re going as fast as possible in scaling domestic production.

John Collison

You’re making the solar cells at Tesla?

Elon Musk

Both Tesla and SpaceX have a mandate to get to 100 gigawatts a year of solar.

John Collison

Speaking of the annual capacity, I’m curious, in five years time let’s say, what will the installed capacity be on Earth…?

Elon Musk

Five years is a long time.

John Collison

And in space? I deliberately pick five years because it’s after your “once we’re up and running” threshold. So in five years time what’s the on-Earth versus in-space installed AI capacity?

Elon Musk

If you say five years from now, I think probably AI in space will be launching every year the sum total of all AI on Earth. Meaning, five years from now, my prediction is we will launch and be operating every year more AI in space than the cumulative total on Earth.

John Collison

Which is...

Elon Musk

I would expect it to be at least, five years from now, a few hundred gigawatts per year of AI in space and rising. I think you can get to around a terawatt a year of AI in space before you start having fuel supply challenges for the rocket.

John Collison

Okay, but you think you can get hundreds of gigawatts per year in five years time?

Elon Musk

Yes.

Dwarkesh Patel

So 100 gigawatts, depending on the specific power of the whole system with solar arrays and radiators and everything, is on the order of 10,000 Starship launches.

Elon Musk

Yes.

Dwarkesh Patel

You want to do that in one year. So that’s like one Starship launch every hour. That’s happening in this city? Walk me through a world where there’s a Starship launch every single hour.

Elon Musk

I mean, that’s actually a lower rate compared to airlines, aircraft.

Dwarkesh Patel

There’s a lot of airports.

Elon Musk

A lot of airports.

Dwarkesh Patel

And you’ve got to launch into the polar orbit.

Elon Musk

No, it doesn’t have to be polar. There’s some value to sun-synchronous, but I think actually, if you just go high enough, you start getting out of Earth’s shadow.

Dwarkesh Patel

How many physical Starships are needed to do 10,000 launches a year?

Elon Musk

I don’t think we’ll need more than... You could probably do it with as few as 20 or 30. It really depends on how quickly… The ship has to go around the Earth and the ground track for the ship has to come back over the launch pad. So if you can use a ship every, say 30 hours, you could do it with 30 ships. But we’ll make more ships than that. SpaceX is gearing up to do 10,000 launches a year, and maybe even 20 or 30,000 launches a year.

Dwarkesh Patel

Is the idea to become basically a hyperscaler, become an Oracle, and lend this capacity to other people? Presumably, SpaceX is the one launching all this. So, SpaceX is going to become a hyperscaler?

Elon Musk

Hyper-hyper. If some of my predictions come true, SpaceX will launch more AI than the cumulative amount on Earth of everything else combined.

Dwarkesh Patel

Is this mostly inference or?

Elon Musk

Most AI will be inference. Already, inference for the purpose of training is most training.

John Collison

There’s a narrative that the change in discussion around a SpaceX IPO is because previously SpaceX was very capital efficient. It wasn’t that expensive to develop. Even though it sounds expensive, it’s actually very capital efficient in how it runs.

Whereas now you’re going to need more capital than just can be raised in the private markets. The private markets can accommodate raises of—as we’ve seen from the AI labs—tens of billions of dollars, but not beyond that. Is it that you’ll just need more than tens of billions of dollars per year? That’s why you’d take it public?

Elon Musk

I have to be careful about saying things about companies that might go public.

Dwarkesh Patel

That’s never been a problem for you, Elon.

Elon Musk

There’s a price to pay for these things.

John Collison

Make some general statements for us about the depth of the capital markets between public and private markets.

Elon Musk

There’s a lot more capital available...

Dwarkesh Patel

Very general.

Elon Musk

There’s obviously a lot more capital available in the public markets than private. It might be 100x more capital, but it’s way more than 10x.

John Collison

Isn’t it also the case that with things that tend to be very capital intensive—if you look at, say, real estate as a huge industry, that raises a lot of money each year at an industry level—they tend to be debt financed because by the time you’re deploying that much money, you actually have a pretty—

Elon Musk

You have a clear revenue stream.

John Collison

Exactly, and a near-term return. You see this even with the data center build-outs, which are famously being financed by the private credit industry. Why not just debt finance?

Elon Musk

Speed is important. I’m generally going to do the thing that... I just repeatedly tackle the limiting factor. Whatever the limiting factor is on speed, I’m going to tackle that. If capital is the limiting factor, then I’ll solve for capital. If it’s not the limiting factor, I’ll solve for something else.

Dwarkesh Patel

Based on your statements about Tesla and being public, I wouldn’t have guessed that you thought the way to move fast is to be public.

Elon Musk

Normally, I would say that’s true. Like I said, I’d like to talk about it in some more detail, but the problem is if you talk about public companies before they become public, you get into trouble, and then you have to delay your offering.

John Collison

And as you said, you’re solving for speed.

Elon Musk

Yes, exactly. You can’t hype companies that might go public. So that’s why we have to be a little careful here. But we can talk about physics. The way you think about scaling long-term is that Earth only receives about half a billionth of the Sun’s energy. The Sun is essentially all the energy. This is a very important point to appreciate because sometimes people will talk about modular nuclear reactors or various fusion on Earth.

But you have to step back a second and say, if you’re going to climb the Kardashev scale and harness some nontrivial percentage of the sun’s energy… Let’s say you wanted to harness a millionth of the sun’s energy, which sounds pretty small. That would be about, call it roughly, 100,000x more electricity than we currently generate on Earth for all of civilization. Give or take an order of magnitude.

Obviously, the only way to scale is to go to space with solar. Launching from Earth, you can get to about a terawatt per year. Beyond that, you want to launch from the moon. You want to have a mass driver on the moon. With that mass driver on the moon, you could do probably a petawatt per year.

Dwarkesh Patel

We’re talking these kinds of numbers, terawatts of compute. Presumably, whether you’re talking about land or space, far, far before this point, you run into... Maybe the solar panels are more efficient, but you still need the chips. You still need the logic and the memory and so forth.

Elon Musk

You’re going to need to build a lot more chips and make them much cheaper.

Dwarkesh Patel

Right now the world has maybe 20-25 gigawatts of compute. How are we getting a terawatt of logic by 2030?

Elon Musk

I guess we’re going to need some very big chip fabs.

Dwarkesh Patel

Tell me about it.

Elon Musk

I’ve mentioned publicly the idea of doing a sort of a TeraFab, Tera being the new Giga.

Dwarkesh Patel

I feel like the naming scheme of Tesla, which has been very catchy, is you looking at the metric scale. At what level of the stack are you? Are you building the clean room and then partnering with an existing fab to get the process technology and buying the tools from them? What is the plan there?

Elon Musk

Well, you can’t partner with existing fabs because they can’t output enough. The chip volume is too low.

Dwarkesh Patel

But for the process technology?

John Collison

Partner for the IP.

Elon Musk

The fabs today all basically use machines from like five companies. So you’ve got ASML, Tokyo Electron, KLA-Tencor, et cetera. So at first, I think you’d have to get equipment from them and then modify it or work with them to increase the volume. But I think you’d have to build perhaps in a different way. The logical thing to do is to use conventional equipment in an unconventional way to get to scale, and then start modifying the equipment to increase the rate.

John Collison

Boring Company-style.

Elon Musk

Yeah. You sort of buy an existing boring machine and then figure out how to dig tunnels in the first place and then design a much better machine that’s some orders of magnitude faster.

John Collison

Here’s a very simple lens. We can categorize technologies and how hard they are. One categorization could be to look at things that China has not succeeded in doing. If you look at Chinese manufacturing, they’re still behind on leading-edge chips and still behind on leading-edge turbine engines and things like that.

So does the fact that China has not successfully replicated TSMC give you any pause about the difficulty? Or do you think that’s not true for some reason?

Elon Musk

It’s not that they have not replicated TSMC, they have not replicated ASML. That’s the limiting factor.

John Collison

So you think it’s just the sanctions, essentially?

Elon Musk

Yeah, China would be outputting vast numbers of chips if they could buy 2-3 nanometers.

John Collison

But couldn’t they up to relatively recently buy them?

Elon Musk

No.

John Collison

Okay.

Elon Musk

The ASML ban has been in place for a while. But I think China’s going to be making pretty compelling chips in three or four years.

John Collison

Would you consider making the ASML machines?

Elon Musk

“I don’t know yet” is the right answer. To reach a large volume in, say, 36 months, to match the rocket payload to orbit… If we’re doing a million tons to orbit in, let’s say three or four years from now, something like that… We’re doing 100 kilowatts per ton. So that means we need at least 100 gigawatts per year of solar. We’ll need an equivalent amount of chips. You need 100 gigawatts worth of chips. You’ve got to match these things: the mass to orbit, the power generation, and the chips.

I’d say my biggest concern actually is memory. The path to creating logic chips is more obvious than the path to having sufficient memory to support logic chips. That’s why you see DDR prices going ballistic and these memes. You’re marooned on a desert island. You write “Help me” on the sand. Nobody comes. You write “DDR RAM.” Ships come swarming in.

Dwarkesh Patel

I’d love to hear your manufacturing philosophy around fabs. I know nothing about the topic.

Elon Musk

I don’t know how to build a fab yet. I’ll figure it out. Obviously, I’ve never built a fab.

Dwarkesh Patel

It sounds like you think the process knowledge of these 10,000 PhDs in Taiwan who know exactly what gas goes in the plasma chamber and what settings to put on the tool, you can just delete those steps. Fundamentally, it’s about getting the clean room, getting the tools, and figuring it out.

Elon Musk

I don’t think it’s PhDs. It’s mostly people who are not PhDs. Most engineering is done by people who don’t have PhDs. Do you guys have PhDs?

John Collison

No.

Elon Musk

Okay.

John Collison

We also haven’t successfully built any fabs, so you shouldn’t be coming to us for fab advice.

Elon Musk

I don’t think you need PhDs for that stuff. But you do need competent personnel. Right now, Tesla is pedal to the metal, max production of going as fast as possible to get Tesla AI5 chip design into production and then reaching scale. That’ll probably happen around the second quarter-ish of next year, hopefully. AI6 would hopefully follow less than a year later. We’ve secured all the chip fab production that we can.

John Collison

Yes. But you’re currently limited on TSMC fab capacity.

Elon Musk

Yeah. We’ll be using TSMC Taiwan, Samsung Korea, TSMC Arizona, Samsung Texas. And we still—

John Collison

You’ve booked out all the capacity.

Elon Musk

Yes. I ask TSMC or Samsung, “okay, what’s the timeframe to get to volume production?” The point is, you’ve got to build the fab and you’ve got to start production, then you’ve got to climb the yield curve and reach volume production at high yield.

That, from start to finish, is a five-year period. So the limiting factor is chips. The limiting factor once you can get to space is chips, but the limiting factor before you can get to space is power.

Dwarkesh Patel

Why don’t you do the Jensen thing and just prepay TSMC to build more fabs for you?

Elon Musk

I’ve already told them that.

Dwarkesh Patel

But they won’t take your money? What’s going on?

Elon Musk

They’re building fabs as fast as they can. So is Samsung. They’re pedal to the metal. They’re going balls to the wall, as fast as they can. It’s still not fast enough. Like I said, I think towards the end of this year, chip production will probably outpace the ability to turn chips on. But once you can get to space and unlock the power constraint, you can now do hundreds of gigawatts per year of power in space.

Again, bearing in mind that average power usage in the US is 500 gigawatts. So if you’re launching, say 200 gigawatts, a year to space, you’re sort of lapping the US every two and a half years. All US electricity production, this is a very huge amount.

Between now and then, the constraint for server-side compute, concentrated compute, will be electricity. My guess is that people start getting to the point where they can’t turn the chips on for large clusters towards the end of this year. The chips are going to be piling up and won’t be able to be turned on.

Now for edge compute it’s a different story. For Tesla, the AI5 chip is going into our Optimus robot. If you have AI edge compute, that’s distributed power. Now the power is distributed over a large area. It’s not concentrated. If you can charge at night, you can actually use the grid much more effectively.

Because the actual peak power production in the US is over 1,000 gigawatts. But the average power usage, because the day-night cycle, is 500. So if you can charge at night, there’s an incremental 500 gigawatts that you can generate at night.

So that’s why Tesla, for edge compute, is not constrained. We can make a lot of chips to make a very large number of robots and cars. But if you try to concentrate that compute, you’re going to have a lot of trouble turning it on.

Dwarkesh Patel

What I find remarkable about the SpaceX business is the end goal is to get to Mars, but you keep finding ways on the way there to keep generating incremental revenue to get to the next stage and the next stage.

So for Falcon 9, it’s Starlink. Now for Starship, it is potentially going to be orbital data centers. You find these infinitely elastic use cases of your next rocket, and your next rocket, and next scale up.

Elon Musk

You can see how this might seem like a simulation to me.

Or am I someone’s avatar in a video game or something? Because what are the odds that all these crazy things should be happening?

I mean, rockets and chips and robots and space solar power. Not to mention the mass driver on the moon. I really want to see that.

Can you imagine some mass driver that’s just going like shoom shoom? It’s sending solar-powered AI satellites into space one after another at two and a half kilometers per second, just shooting them into deep space. That would be a sight to see. I mean, I’d watch that.

John Collison

Just like a live stream of it on a webcam?

Elon Musk

Yeah, yeah, just one after another, just shooting AI satellites into deep space, a billion or 10 billion tons a year.

John Collison

I’m sorry, you manufacture the satellites on the moon?

Elon Musk

Yeah.

John Collison

I see. So you send the raw materials to the moon and then manufacture them there.

Elon Musk

Well, the lunar soil is 20% silicon or something like that. So you can mine the silicon on the moon, refine it, and create the solar cells and the radiators on the moon. You make the radiators out of aluminum. So there’s plenty of silicon and aluminum on the moon to make the cells and the radiators.

The chips you could send from Earth because they’re pretty light. Maybe at some point you make them on the moon, too. Like I said, it does seem like a sort of a video game situation where it’s difficult but not impossible to get to the next level. I don’t see any way that you could do 500-1,000 terawatts per year launched from Earth.

Dwarkesh Patel

I agree.

Elon Musk

But you could do that from the Moon.

Grok and alignment
Dwarkesh Patel

Can I zoom out and ask about the SpaceX mission? I think you’ve said that we’ve got to get to Mars so we can make sure that if something happens to Earth, civilization, consciousness, and all that survives.

Elon Musk

Depending on what your yield assumptions are, that tells you how many chips you need to make. If you’re going to have 100 gigawatts of power, you need 100 million chips that are running at a kilowatt sustained, per reticle. Basic math.

Dwarkesh Patel

100 million chips depends on… If you look at the die size of something like Blackwell GPUs or something, and how many you can get out of a wafer, you can get on the order of dozens or less per wafer. So basically, this is a world where if we’re putting that out every single year, you’re producing millions of wafers a month. That’s the plan with TeraFab? Millions of wafers a month of advanced process nodes?

Elon Musk

Yeah it could be north of a million or something. You’ve got to do the memory too.

Dwarkesh Patel

Are you going to make a memory fab?

Elon Musk

I think the TeraFab’s got to do memory. It’s got to do logic, memory, and packaging.

Dwarkesh Patel

I’m very curious how somebody gets started. This is the most complicated thing man has ever made. Obviously, if anybody’s up to the task, you’re up to the task. So you realize it’s a bottleneck, and you go to your engineers. What do you tell them to do? “I want a million wafers a month in 2030.”

Elon Musk

That’s right. That’s exactly what I want.

Dwarkesh Patel

Do you call ASML? What is the next step?

John Collison

No so much to ask.

Elon Musk

We make a little fab and see what happens. Make our mistakes at a small scale and then make a big one.

Dwarkesh Patel

Is a little fab done?

Elon Musk

No, it’s not done. We’re not going to keep that cat in the bag. That cat’s going to come out of the bag. There’ll be drones hovering over the bloody thing. You’ll be able to see its construction progress on X in real time.

Look, I don’t know, we could just flounder in failure, to be fair. Success is not guaranteed. Since we want to try to make something like 100 million… We want 100 gigawatts of power and chips that can take 100 gigawatts by 2030. We’ll take as many chips as our suppliers will give us. I’ve actually said this to TSMC and Samsung and Micron: “please build more fabs faster”. We will guarantee to buy the output of those fabs. So they’re already moving as fast as they can. It’s us plus them.

John Collison

There’s a narrative that the people doing AI want a very large number of chips as quickly as possible. Then many of the input suppliers, the fabs, but also the turbine manufacturers, are not ramping up production very quickly.

Elon Musk

No, they’re not.

John Collison

The explanation you hear is that they’re dispositionally conservative. They’re Taiwanese or German, as the story may be. They just don’t believe... Is that really the explanation or is there something else?

Elon Musk

Well, it’s reasonable to... If somebody’s been in the computer memory business for 30 or 40 years…

John Collison

They’ve seen cycles.

Elon Musk

They’ve seen boom and bust 10 times. That’s a lot of layers of scar tissue. During the boom times, it looks like everything is going to be great forever. Then the crash happens and they’re desperately trying to avoid bankruptcy. Then there’s another boom and another crash.

John Collison

Are there other ideas you think others should go pursue that you’re not for whatever reasons right now?

Elon Musk

There are a few companies that are pursuing new ways of doing chips, but they’re just not scaling fast.

John Collison

I don’t even mean within AI, I mean just generally.

Elon Musk

People should do the thing where they find that they’re highly motivated to do that thing, as opposed to some idea that I suggest. They should do the thing that they find personally interesting and motivating to do.

But going back to the limiting factor… I used that phrase about 100 times. The current limiting factor that I see in the three to four year timeframe, it’s chips. In the one year timeframe, it’s energy, power production, electricity. It’s not clear to me that there’s enough usable electricity to turn on all the AI chips that are being made.

Towards the end of this year, I think people are going to have real trouble turning on... The chip output will exceed the ability to turn chips on.

Dwarkesh Patel

What’s your plan to deal with that world?

Elon Musk

We’re trying to accelerate electricity production. I guess that’s maybe one of the reasons that xAI will be maybe the leader, hopefully the leader. We’ll be able to turn on more chips than other people can turn on, faster, because we’re good at hardware.

Generally, the innovations from the corporations that call themselves labs, the ideas tend to flow… It’s rare to see that there’s more than about a six-month difference. The ideas travel back and forth with the people.

So I think you sort of hit the hardware wall and then whichever company can scale hardware the fastest will be the leader. So I think xAI will be able to scale hardware the fastest and therefore most likely will be the leader.

John Collison

You joked or were self-conscious about using the “limiting factor” phrase again. But I actually think there’s something deep here. If you look at a lot of things we’ve touched on over the course of it, it’s maybe a good note to end on. If you think of a senescent, low-agency company, it would have some bottleneck and not really be doing anything about it.

Marc Andreessen had the line of, “most people are willing to endure any amount of chronic pain to avoid acute pain”. It feels like a lot of the cases we’re talking about are just leaning into the acute pain, whatever it is. “Okay, we got to figure out how to work with steel, or we got to figure out how to run the chips in space.” We’ll take some near-term acute pain to actually solve the bottleneck. So that’s kind of a unifying theme.

Elon Musk

I have a high pain threshold. That’s helpful.

John Collison

To solve the bottleneck.

Elon Musk

Yes. One thing I can say is, I think the future is going to be very interesting. As I said at Davos—I think I was on the ground for like three hours or something—it’s better to err on the side of optimism and be wrong than err on the side of pessimism and be right, for quality of life. You’ll be happier if you err on the side of optimism rather than erring on the side of pessimism. So I recommend erring on the side of optimism.

John Collison

Here’s to that.

Dwarkesh Patel

Cool. Elon, thanks for doing this.

John Collison

Thank you.

Elon Musk

All right, thanks guys. All right.

John Collison

Great stamina.

Dwarkesh Patel

Hopefully this didn’t count as a pain in the pain tolerance.]

items.content: Bridging the divide between deterministic physics-based control and policy-driven adaptation, Boston Dynamics released a video today showing its Atlas humanoid using wheels to move around. The “experiment” combined classical model-based motor control with whole-body reinforcement learning to maintain dynamic stability across unstructured, real-world terrain. In the video, Andy Wu, controls engineer for Atlas at Boston Dynamics, highlights some recent experiments that he executed by attaching wheels to Atlas’ legs. Boston Dynamics said “a wheeled Atlas isn’t a product. It’s a research testbed.” Wu’s intention was to push the actuation to its limits. Another goal of the experiment was to understand unstructured environment adaptability. Wu addresses the limitations of purely model-based control when navigating unpredictable, real-world conditions that are difficult to model or simulate. Through a whole-body reinforcement learning (RL) policy, Atlas demonstrates that it can process real-time proprioceptive feedback and velocity commands. The experiment also outputs dynamic pose and force adjustments to mitigate unmodeled disturbances and non-ideal contact states. Boston Dynamics attached wheels to the feet of the Atlas humanoid for a set of controls engineering experiments. | Credit: Boston Dynamics Atlas moves like a skater In addition to learning how to move with wheels for feet, Atlas also performs pirouettes and various aggressive actuation maneuvers. This demonstrates that Atlas can smoothly switch between fast rolling on flat terrain and articulated legged motion over obstacles or irregular surfaces. Wu trained the system in sim. The system learned all of the behaviors in sim and executed them in real life, with surprising accuracy, according to Wu. Wu said converting Atlas’ locomotion style was “wonderfully simple.” A single custom adapter mounts an off-the-shelf scooter rim onto Atlas’ existing ankle actuator, and that’s the only new part in the whole build. Because Atlas was designed from the start to be produced at high volume and to be easy to service, Wu said the retrofit was about as involved as swapping a wheel on a bicycle. The software side was just as straightforward, he said. Each wheel is modeled as an “ankle” that can spin continuously, so all Wu had to do was take the baseline robot model and swap the feet out for wheels. Real-world implications for humanoid operation The next question that Wu intends to answer is the policy response to failed actuators. This is key to safety and to understanding how the system will respond to a system failure. The primary takeaway for Wu and the controls engineering team at Boston Dynamics is to understand control synergy. The video demonstrates that merging classical motor controls (for baseline stability) with whole-body RL (for reactive adaptation) yields superior real-world agility compared to using either method alone. Wheels vs. legs debate continues Boston Dynamics’ latest Atlas experiment adds another interesting data point to the ongoing wheels-versus-legs debate in humanoid robotics. While many companies are developing wheeled humanoids, others are committed to legs for navigating environments designed for people. Agility Robotics recently said it is also exploring wheeled robots as part of a broader family of human-centric, multipurpose platforms. Co-founder and Chief Robot Officer Jonathan Hurst said Digit likely won’t get wheels, but the company is exploring other wheeled configurations. Again, Boston Dynamics said a wheeled Atlas is a research testbed, not a product. Still, experiments like this raise an interesting question about how much of the humanoid form factor needs to be human-like to be commercially useful. We’ll be watching to see where the industry goes next. The experiments come as Boston Dynamics prepares to ramp up Atlas testing at Hyundai facilities and continues developing the humanoid’s capabilities, including its new four-fingered gripper . The Robot Report will be watching how these developments translate into real-world deployments. Submit your innovation now! items.content: Wi-Fi connectivity needs to be reliable for real-time mobile robot management. Source: Synaptics An autonomous mobile robot or AMR may cross dozens of Wi-Fi coverage zones during a single shift. Each transition creates a small but potentially consequential communications problem: How does the robot find its next access point without interrupting the connection it is already using? The answer matters because AMRs , industrial inspection robots, warehouse automation, and healthcare service robots increasingly depend on continuous connectivity for sensor data, telemetry, and control. In a conventional Wi-Fi architecture, the primary communication radio must periodically stop transmitting and receiving application traffic while it searches for alternative access points. That creates a tradeoff among connectivity, latency, power consumption, and roaming performance. A dedicated scan architecture separates network discovery from application traffic. The robot can monitor its wireless environment continuously while the primary radio maintains the active connection. One implementation, Synaptics Scan Core, uses a low-power wireless subsystem to monitor neighboring access points while the primary Wi-Fi radio remains dedicated to application traffic. This separation can support faster roaming decisions, lower latency, reduced packet loss, and more efficient scanning. As robots become more mobile, roaming is mission-critical Robots are becoming more connected and autonomous across manufacturing , logistics , healthcare , retail , and service environments. As they move through larger and more complex facilities, reliable wireless connectivity and fast roaming become core design requirements rather than secondary networking considerations. Unlike stationary Wi-Fi devices, robots move continually between coverage areas while maintaining video, AI inference, telemetry, and fleet-management communications. These combined demands make mobile robotics a strong use case for dedicated scanning architectures. Modern robots also support increasingly demanding wireless workloads, including HD and multi-camera video , simultaneous localization and mapping ( SLAM ), AI-assisted navigation , predictive maintenance, and remote operation. Wireless connectivity has therefore evolved from a convenience into a critical operational subsystem. Submit your innovation now! Mobility poses challenges A mobile robot must maintain application traffic as it moves between Wi-Fi coverage zones. A warehouse robot may roam dozens or even hundreds of times during a shift. Each roaming event can introduce: Increased latency Packet loss Video disruption Delayed control responses Reduced productivity Common performance targets for robotics deployments include: Requirement Typical Target Roaming latency <80 ms Sustained throughput 20 Mbps Packet loss during roaming <2% For many autonomous systems, meeting these targets is important to safe and efficient operation. Key requirements and pain points Although stakeholders evaluate robotics systems differently, several wireless performance measures consistently emerge as critical. Roaming latency A typical roaming process includes the following steps: Network discovery Candidate evaluation Authentication Security key exchange Reassociation Each step adds delay. In robotics applications, excessive roaming latency can affect navigation, fleet coordination, teleoperation , and machine-vision performance. Packet loss Even brief connectivity interruptions can affect AMR operations and data transfer. Robots often require communications performance that is consistent and predictable enough for real-time operation. Power consumption AMRs must continuously balance battery performance and energy efficiency. Aggressive scanning improves roaming responsiveness but typically increases power consumption. Dense RF environments Warehouses, factories, airports, and hospitals often contain many access points, multiple wireless protocols, and significant RF reflections. These conditions place additional demands on roaming algorithms. Dedicated scanning can address mobile robot connectivity Traditional Wi-Fi clients use the primary communication radio for both application traffic and network discovery. During a background scan, the radio temporarily leaves its serving channel to look for neighboring access points, interrupting active traffic and potentially adding delay or packet loss. A dedicated scan architecture assigns continuous monitoring of the wireless environment to a separate low-power resource. The primary Wi-Fi radio can remain focused on application traffic while candidate access points are identified in advance. Source: Synaptics Synaptics Scan Core is one implementation of this general architectural approach. A dedicated scan resource removes this contention between active communications and network discovery. Source: Synaptics Traditional Wi-Fi versus Scan Core Conventional Wi-Fi Dedicated Scan Core Main communication radio performs scanning Dedicated Scan Core performs scanning User traffic interrupted during scans User traffic radio is not interrupted by scan operations Reactive roaming Proactive roaming Higher scan power Lower scan power Longer roaming time Faster roaming Periodic access point discovery Continuous AP discovery Key benefits Continuous network awareness: The scan radio continuously monitors neighboring channels while the primary radio remains connected. Faster roaming decisions: Candidate access points are discovered before signal quality degrades. Lower packet loss: Active communications continue during background scanning. More predictable performance: Roaming behavior becomes more consistent and predictable. Improved power efficiency: Background scanning can be optimized without disrupting active communications. Instead of waiting for connectivity to deteriorate, the wireless subsystem can prepare for the next roaming event while application traffic continues on the primary radio. Measured Scan Core benefits Synaptics said its platform characterization measured substantial improvements in scanning efficiency: Metric Improvement Scan time Up to 65% faster Overall scan duration Approximately 40% shorter Scan power Up to 75% lower Scan current Up to 77% lower Source: Synaptics robotics platform characterization In a mobile robot, these improvements can contribute to faster roaming, lower scan energy, longer battery life, and steadier application traffic. Actual results will depend on the platform, network topology, traffic load, and RF environment. Applying dedicated scanning to mobile robots Commercial connectivity platforms are beginning to incorporate dedicated scanning. For instance, Synaptics offers an integrated platform combining Wi-Fi 7, dual Bluetooth 6.0, and IEEE 802.15.4, as well as multi-band operation across 2.4, 5, and 6 GHz. Within that platform, Scan Core provides a dedicated scan resource that operates independently of the primary WLAN subsystem. This allows scanning and active communications to occur simultaneously rather than compete for the same radio. Multi-band awareness The platform evaluates candidate access points across multiple frequency bands, helping the robot maintain connectivity as it moves through a facility. Fast channel switching The architecture supports rapid transitions between the main and scan resources. On the Synaptics robotics validation platform, switching between resources was measured on the order of microseconds. Roaming test results Figure 3 summarizes the minimum and maximum measured roaming times across three representative scenarios. In Synaptics platform testing, all results remained below the 80 ms target while continuous 20 Mbps UDP traffic was maintained: Source: Synaptics Wireless mobility becomes part of robot performance As AMRs take on more complex workloads and operate across larger, denser environments, wireless mobility becomes part of the robot’s performance envelope. Roaming affects productivity, fleet efficiency, the user experience, and, in some applications, safe operation. Conventional Wi-Fi makes the communication radio divide its time between application traffic and network discovery. A dedicated scan architecture separates those functions, allowing the robot to identify its next connection without interrupting the one it is already using. Dedicated scanning and Wi-Fi 7 enhanced Multi-Link Single Radio ( eMLSR ) address different parts of wireless mobility. Dedicated scanning improves awareness of nearby access points; eMLSR improves how the device uses multiple links. Together, they can make roaming faster and more predictable without forcing designers to trade application performance against network awareness. In Synaptics internal validation, eMLSR delivered up to a 10x latency improvement over single-link operation under congested conditions. Results vary with network topology, traffic load, and RF conditions. eMLSR can provide many multi-link operation latency benefits without requiring multiple fully active radios. Synaptics says Scan Core can help mobile robots maintain coverage. Source: Synaptics Glossary Autonomous mobile robot An AMR can navigating and performing tasks using sensors, AI, and wireless connectivity without requiring fixed guidance infrastructure or direct human control. Access point An AP is a wireless networking device that provides Wi-Fi connectivity to client devices within a coverage area. Enhanced Multi-Link Single Radio eMLSR is a Wi-Fi 7 capability that enables a single radio to intelligently utilize multiple wireless links, improving latency, reliability, and power efficiency. Fleet management Software and network infrastructure used to monitor, coordinate, and manage multiple AMRs operating within the same environment. Latency The time required for data to travel between devices. Low and predictable latency is critical for real-time robotics applications. Multi-Link Operation MLO is a Wi-Fi 7 feature that allows communication over multiple wireless links, improving throughput, reliability, and network efficiency. Packet loss Data packets that fail to reach their destination. Excessive packet loss can interrupt video, telemetry, and real-time control. Roaming The process by which a Wi-Fi client transitions from one access point to another while maintaining network connectivity. Scan Core A dedicated low-power wireless receive subsystem that continuously monitors the wireless environment while the primary Wi-Fi radio remains dedicated to application traffic. By separating network awareness from communications, Scan Core enables faster roaming, lower latency, reduced packet loss, and improved power efficiency, according to Synaptics. Simultaneous Localization and Mapping SLAM is a navigation technique that enables a robot to build a map of its environment while simultaneously determining its own position within that map. Simultaneous Transmit and Receive STR is a Wi-Fi 7 Multi-Link Operation mode that enables simultaneous transmission and reception over multiple wireless links, maximizing throughput and reducing latency. User Datagram Protocol UDP is a lightweight transport protocol used for real-time applications such as video streaming, voice, gaming, and telemetry. Unlike TCP, UDP does not retransmit lost packets, making it well suited for measuring network latency, packet loss, and roaming performance in wireless systems. Wi-Fi 7 The latest generation of Wi-Fi technology ( IEEE 802.11be ) introduced features such as MLO, wider channel bandwidths, lower latency, and improved efficiency in dense wireless environments. About the author Mikko Niemi is a product manager for wireless products at Synaptics Inc. He has more than 15 years of experience across industrial Internet of Things ( IIoT ), semiconductor, and software-as-a-service (SaaS) sectors. Niemi specializes in building and scaling intelligent, data-driven platforms that power connected infrastructure, smart energy systems, and next-generation industrial applications. He previously worked at Lantronix, where he led a portfolio that included industrial IoT gateways, cloud-based, SaaS device management platforms, and global connectivity services—delivering edge-to-cloud systems that integrate real-time telemetry, AI/machine learning analytics, and robust security at scale. Niemi previosly held management roles at Silicon Labs and Landis+Gyr. He holds an MBA and a Master’s in electronics engineering. items.content: High-precision manufacturing was once considered something exclusive to large corporations. However, advances in robotic integration and automated manufacturing have changed this perception. Sophisticated capabilities are becoming accessible to midmarket and smaller operations. This shift has led to a more even competitive landscape. Smaller manufacturers have an opportunity to reach new levels of accuracy and efficiency. Today’s robotic systems can help these producers modernize targeted workflows without overhauling their entire production operations. Robotic innovations drive efficiency for manufacturers The evolution of robotics has led to more democratized precision manufacturing processes. This is evident across industrial robots and agile collaborative robots . Key benefits of these innovations can include: Cost and footprint: The potential for lower investment costs and compact designs can make robotic systems economically viable. It can also simplify integration into existing layouts. Enhanced programming: Intuitive interfaces and lead-through teaching methods support quick deployment and reconfiguration. This reduces the training typically required for operators without robotics expertise. Sensors and AI -driven capabilities: Sensors, such as vision systems and force-torque sensors, can be integrated with AI. This enables robots to understand, react and adapt with precision. Safety and collaboration: Cobots can work safely alongside humans without extensive guarding. This fosters a flexible human-robot workforce that combines optimal utilization and human dexterity. These advancements mean that midmarket manufacturers can overcome hurdles like skilled labor shortages, rising costs, and quality demands. Submit your innovation now! Real-world impact of robotic integration for precision manufacturers Here are some use cases that show how a diverse range of manufacturers have taken advantage of recent advances in robotics. 1. SCHUNK R-C2 automation for flexible production Torneria Novoletto is an Italian organization specializing in sophisticated components for the chemical, medical , and pharmaceutical sectors. The company faced obstacles in achieving high precision and process reliability for medium-sized batches. It implemented SCHUNK’s R-C2 automation concept , integrating advanced clamping devices and grippers with robotic handling. Introducing this system helped to support high operational flexibility. Setup and changeover times were also significantly reduced because the SCHUNK R-C2 allows the continuous handling of workpiece sizes and automated reclamping. This innovative robotic integration has helped Torneria Novoletto to pursue an unmanned 24/7 operation, increase machine utilization, and mitigate shortages of skilled labor. Torneria Novoletto shows the compact efficiency of the R-C2 automation. Source: SCHUNK 2. Cobot integration for part marking Telesis, a leading provider of industrial marking solutions, integrated its part marking technology with systems from Universal Robots . The company offers advanced laser and dot peen markers. When a Telesis laser marking system is integrated with a UR force- and power-limited robot arm, it creates a precise and flexible method of identifying automated parts. Innovations like this ensure that systems can be safely deployed alongside human workers. Robotic integrations have provided Telesis with a streamlined marking process without complex safety enclosures, consistent high-quality marking on various materials and part geometries, and added traceability and quality control. Telesis demonstrates integrated laser-marking systems with robotic control. Source: Universal Robots 3. FANUC M-20 robots enhance throughput and scale Northern Kentucky Machine (NKM), a flexible job shop, experienced labor shortages and production capacity challenges. Its strategic response included the use of automated manufacturing solutions, such as deploying FANUC M-20 Series industrial robots. By using Automation Within Reach’s (AWR) “RC-2” CNC machine-tending system, the integration increased NKM’s throughput and machine utilization. Operators quickly adapted to programming and running these robotic cells. This helped to enable “lights-out” manufacturing for longer runs, freeing up human workers for other tasks. The FANUC robots have provided NKM with the scalability needed to pursue and take on larger projects, deliver consistent part quality, drive growth, and compete with other midsize organizations. NKM used the M-20 Series robot to boost the efficiency of human workers. Source: FANUC 4. ActiNav enables bin picking and legacy equipment extension PrecisionForm Inc. is a producer of small custom metal parts. It faced the challenge of automating bin picking for CNC machines. By deploying Universal Robots’ ActiNav system , PrecisionForm integrated a UR5 cobot with advanced vision and path-planning capabilities. This approach led to reliable part picking from deep bins that were then loaded into CNC machines. Challenging geometries were less of an issue, and operators were freed up to manage multiple machines. The UR cobots helped reduce labor challenges and extend the lifespan of older CNC equipment. By adding a relatively inexpensive robotic solution, PrecisionForm Inc gained additional utility from existing machinery, increased the potential return on investment (ROI) as a midmarket operation, and improved daily production. Uses can easily deploy and calibrate the ActiNav system, says UR. Source: Universal Robots Capabilities evolve for midmarket manufacturers The accessibility of precision manufacturing marks a crucial moment for many industries. Robotic integration is no longer exclusive to the world’s largest enterprises. Innovations offering ultra-high accuracy and consistent quality are now economically and operationally viable for midsized manufacturers. The benefits that organizations such as Telesis, Torneria Novoletto, NKM, and PrecisionForm now have shown that modern robotics can drive sustainable growth. Robotic solutions continue to evolve. As they do, the advantages of automated manufacturing will grow alongside those changes. With thoughtful and careful implementation, a new generation of agile and highly precise manufacturers will be waiting to reap the benefits of this exciting new world. He has a great passion for the stories he covers and for writing in general. This article is posted with permission. items.content: The new Stretch features an updated modular design that enables “plug and play” part swaps. | Source: Boston Dynamics Boston Dynamics Inc. this week unveiled Stretch Gen 2, the latest generation of its autonomous mobile trailer unloading robot. With over 100,000 operating hours and tens of millions of boxes handled under its belt, the company built the updated robot to maximize uptime and streamline maintenance. Brian Donnelly, the vice president and general manager of logistics robotics at Boston Dynamics, told  The Robot Report that the company has been working on the new version of Stretch for around two and a half years. “When we made the first generation of Stretch, we were focused on trying to get a product out into the market as fast as possible and really get it in customers’ hands and get it operational,” he said. “It was not the easiest to manufacture; there were a lot of components.” “[With Stretch 2], we really were focused on simplification, hardening the robot, and really driving improved reliability and performance,” added Donnelly. “That’s really what drove a lot of our decisions was just making the robot better in every way.” Stretch Gen 2 can unload up to 1,000 cases per hour. This rate is highly dependent on factors such as case weight and how neat or disorderly cases are stacked. It has a multipick feature, a battery that can last two shifts, and a fast charger that can get it to 90% charge in about 75 minutes. The mobile manipulator also features onboard lighting, making it easier to work in dark trailers, and a pre-trained vision system that can detect most packages without programming needed. Stretch’s hardware upgrades improve durability Boston Dynamics geared many of Stretch Gen 2’s upgrades towards reducing downtime and making the robot more durable. For example, the Waltham, Mass.-based company also cut 81% of the internal cabling, around half a mile’s worth. “[Cabling] is weight, it’s cost, and its points of failure, particularly when you have something that’s in constant motion, you’re creating strain on those cables with every motion,” Donnelly said. “If you don’t have good strain relief, you don’t have good ways of managing the cables in the robot. It can cause stress on the cables and then failure.” Donnelly said Hyundai helped the company source a cable harness through its automotive supply chain. This isn’t the only thing Boston Dynamics learned from the automotive industry. Stretch Gen 2 uses heavy-duty automotive-grade connectors. These hold up to the vibration of rapid, high-torque box handling and driving over uneven floors. “In the automotive industry, they have to deal with a lot of real-world challenges in their vehicles. There’s a lot of miles driven dealing with shock and vibration and things like this,” Donnelly said. “As a robot moves around the world, just like a car, if you don’t have latching connectors, then they can sort of wiggle apart. By leveraging those automotive connectors, we’re much more confident that the connectors are going to stay latched together and not pull apart in the field.” The robot also has continuous rotation joints that move beyond 360° so they no longer hit hard stops. This can help prevent previously caused mechanical stress. Donnelly pointed out this also makes the robot more productive, as it can completely optimize its trajectory planning and move in any direction. The emergency stop on the robot now sits lower and is recessed. Boston Dynamics made the exterior panels with new materials so a falling box is far less likely to trip an unintentional safety stoppage or break a panel. How Stretch Gen 2 gets a grip on multiple boxes The gripper is the part of the robot that often deals with the most stress. It’s making contact with all of the the things the robot needs to handle. Stretch Gen 2 features an upgraded gripper with new valve systems and more precise sensing improves grasping and placement to optimize fast-paced picks. “[The new gripper] has a valve in every suction cup, which enables us to pick multiple boxes with a single motion of the arm, which substantially increases our throughput,” Donnelly explained. “If we can pick multiple boxes, with a single motion of the arm, we get much higher throughput because the pick cycle of picking up a box from the floor of a container and place it to a conveyor is dominated by arm movement. So, if we can keep the arm moving and just do more every cycle, that is really effective and improves the rate at which we can unload a truck for our customers.” The new gripper is also better at configuring boxes on the conveyor belt in ways that work best for Boston Dynamics’ customers, and use less power in picking up boxes. “Every cup is individually sensed and actuated, so we know when we have good suction,” said Donnelly. “We only have the valve open to pull suction when we have good contact on a box, so that enables us to reduce the amount of power we’re spending running on the vacuum pump, so we’re not pulling suction through cups that don’t have good contact. It also enables us to, when we pick up those multiple boxes, singulate them onto the conveyor.” Stretch Gen 2 brings service time down to just hours With Stretch Gen 2, Boston Dynamics didn’t just want to reduce the frequency of service calls; it also wanted to make those service calls faster when they do happen. “We didn’t have as much experience from a serviceability perspective as a company when we made the first-generation robot,” Donnelly said. “We’ve since deployed these robots, serviced them in the field, and hired a lot of people who have a lot more experience than we originally did in service. Their input and guidance really helped us to make a robot that’s much more manufacturable and more serviceable.” The robot doesn’t require dynamic cables and complex harnesses. Instead it uses standardized high-strength fasteners to cut down on tool changes and hands-on repair time. For example, the company can perform a full swerve drive swap in just one hour. Before, this process could take an entire day. Stretch Gen 2 also features new onboard diagnostics and maintenance tools. These put more routine service in the hands of a customer’s own maintenance team, so robots stay on the dock with less reliance on outside support. Updated robot continuously improves its performance The new robot runs on a redesigned onboard computing platform that is constantly improving. Boston Dynamics said it will regularly release software updates to bring gains in case detection, motion planning, pick strategies, and world modeling across an entire fleet, with no hardware changes required. Donnelly said that with the company’s most recent update, it saw a 24% increase in unload rate across its fleet of fielded robots. “A lot of our activity on this program is really focused on the software. We’re constantly improving our computer vision capabilities to be able to better perceive boxes and conveyors and container walls, and then really pick boxes and place them to convey more and more productivity over time,” Donnelly said. Right now, Donnelly said Boston Dynamics releases new software, on average, on a monthly basis. Submit your innovation now! How have customers reacted to Gen 2 so far? Donnelly said Boston Dynamics already has Stretch Gen 2 running at multiple customer sites. “Customers are really happy with it, and they’re continuing to rely on it to do its work every day,” said Donnelly. “We’re going into these existing sites and deploying these robots within two weeks. The folks who are taking over operating the robots are the folks who are otherwise doing repetitive heavy lifting of these boxes and containers.” “We put a lot of effort into ensuring that the user experience, from an operator perspective, is really simple. It doesn’t require a ton of training,” he added. “A person can drive the robot into a container, step out of the safety work cell, and they press a big Play button, and then the robot does the rest.” Many of the people working with Stretch used to spend their days unloading heavy boxes from trailers. “Fundamentally, unloading trailers is one of the worst jobs in the warehouse,” Donnelly said. “It can be really hot in a container that’s been sitting in a yard in the summer. It can be super cold in the winter. Then the work itself is moving heavy boxes repeatedly from down low or up high. It puts a lot of strain and stress on people’s bodies.” The post Boston Dynamics built Stretch Gen 2 for reliable, consistent performance appeared first on The Robot Report .

items.content: ABB Robotics has integrated NVIDIA Omniverse libraries into RobotStudio. Source: ABB Robotics Yesterday, ABB Robotics confirmed to The Robot Report that China’s Office of the Working Mechanism for Foreign Investment Security Review has blocked SoftBank Group Corp.’s planned acquisition of ABB Robotics. Regulators had expressed concern that data for training artificial intelligence models could be transferred overseas. ABB Robotics is already a significant manufacturer and provider of robotics in China . The Zurich-based company stated that it and SoftBank are “in close dialogue and are working constructively on the transaction.” Other countries are moving to protect what they view as sovereign physical AI . For instance, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission ( FCC ) recently banned new models of certain connected advanced devices, including legged robots and autonomous mobile robots ( AMRs ). Companies such as Intel and Husqvarna have already received conditional approvals. In addition, the U.S. Department of Commerce last week determined that imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and related components pose a threat to the U.S. economy and national security. This could lead to tariffs . Government investigations can directly affect major robotics and AI companies. European antitrust scrutiny of Amazon’s proposed acquisition of iRobot was one reason why that deal was terminated , with iRobot subsequently entering bankruptcy proceedings. The robotic vacuum pioneer has since been picked up by Shenzhen, China-based Picea Robotics Co. ABB Robotics as focused on automation and AI ABB Robotics claimed that it is the only company whose integrated portfolio includes industrial automation , software, force- and power-limited cobots , and AMRs . The company said its “autonomous versatile robotics” help businesses of all sizes in industries including automotive , electronics , and logistics . ABB Robotics has installed more than 500,000 robots around the world and employs about 7,000 people. Its U.S. headquarters are in Auburn Hills, Mich. In October 2025, parent company ABB said it had agreed to sell its robotics division to Japan-based SoftBank Group Corp. for $5.3 billion. “Considering the intensive competition in traditional robotics, established manufacturers like ABB will need to lead the charge in AI-driven robotics to protect their margins,” said Samantha Mou, a senior analyst at Interact Analysis . “However, achieving this will require significant investment. The substantial long-term R&D costs may be a key factor behind ABB’s decision to sell its robotics business.” “Compared with the other Big 4 vendors [FANUC, KUKA, and Yaskawa], ABB was already quick in combining AI with its products, which is an area where it can have synergy with SoftBank,” Mou told The Robot Report . She said that companies in Europe, Asia, and the Americas are hoping that AI, which has already been used for ease of programming, monitoring, and predictive maintenance, can be generalized to more processes. “AI gives ABB Robotics considerable potential,” said Robert Little , a business development advisor and former chief of robotics strategy at Novanta Inc, on LinkedIn . “But turning that potential into commercially useful systems requires sustained investment. In my humble opinion, backing that investment within ABB becomes a harder decision when robotics has to compete for funding against higher-margin businesses. ABB also saw limited synergies between robotics and the rest of the company.” “SoftBank made sense,” he added. “ABB brings robot manufacturing, application expertise and established customer relationships. SoftBank could bring additional investment and a clear focus on AI.” Sovereign physical AI becomes a strategic concern “Post Astra, robotics data has become more strategic,” posted Financial Times reporter Zijing Wu, in reference to the GPT-6 model that OpenAI released in September and that Chinese AI firms used to train their models. “The NDRC [China’s National Development and Reform Commission] had been concerned about robotics data being transferred overseas, where it could be used to train AI models, including those developed by OpenAI, in which SoftBank is a major investor, sources say,” said Wu on X . Countries have become increasingly aware of the competitive advantage promised by the convergence of automation and AI. “What makes this particularly significant is that industrial robotics is increasingly being viewed not simply as manufacturing equipment, but as strategically important technology at the intersection of automation, data, and AI,” Ash Sharma, managing director of Interact Analysis, told The Robot Report . “China is a critical market for ABB Robotics, so separating the Chinese operation from a global transaction of this scale would be extremely challenging,” he added. “More broadly, this highlights how robotics data, intellectual property, and local manufacturing capability are becoming important considerations in cross-border M&A as physical AI develops.” Ahmed Humayun, head of go to market for defense manufacturing at Gecko Robotics , posted to LinkedIn : “This move reflects Chinese concerns about asset transfers to Japan during a time of heightened Chinese-Japanese tension, but [it] also shows concerns about robotics data generated in China being transferred abroad to train foundation models. The most recent example of China flexing its economic muscle and demonstrating that it has many levers to prevent intellectual property and assets from leaving its soil — even when developed by foreign companies.” “I was worried this might happen,” said Little. “Over the years, I have seen ABB ‘s strength in China grow. Where do we go from here?” “My take: ABB has built a strong presence in China, but heavily subsidized Chinese robot makers are becoming stronger competitors at home and expanding into Europe,” he wrote. “That creates more pressure on pricing and margins that were not that great to begin with fall even further.” “There may still be negotiations that find a way forward,” concluded Little. “For now, ABB is in a pickle.” Submit your innovation now! items.content: Loco-manipulation, which requires mobile manipulators to coordinate locomotion and manipulation over long horizons, is a key capability for large-object rearrangement in applications such as service robotics and warehouse automation. Despite recent progress, reliably executing these tasks remains challenging because performance depends on complex robot-object and object-environment interaction dynamics. Existing approaches address this challenge either through model-based methods, which often require accurate dynamics models, or through learning-based methods, which reduce this requirement but typically assume a fixed or predefined initial grasp. However, different geometrically stable grasps can lead to substantially different downstream manipulation performance. Therefore, we propose Grasp-TAGS, a task-aware grasp selection framework for goal-conditioned large-object rearrangement. We train a unified PPO-based reinforcement learning policy across multiple initial grasp configurations and distill the learned critic into a lightweight grasp utility network that ranks candidate grasps using only the candidate grasp configuration and goal information. At inference time, we select the grasp with the highest predicted downstream utility for the downstream policy to complete the task, before even making a contact. Experiments demonstrate that Grasp-TAGS improves rearrangement success over both fixed single-grasp policies and random grasp selection, achieving an average success rate of 89.84% compared with 79.87% for the best-performing single-grasp policies, an improvement of 9.97 percentage points. Grasp-TAGS also reduces final orientation errors across all evaluated objects. For more qualitative results, refer to the supplementary webpage: https://rpm-lab-umn.github.io/Grasp-TAGS-web-page/
