items.content: The AIhub coffee corner captures the musings of AI experts over a short conversation. This month we ask whether humanoids are the future of robotics. How has the technology evolved recently, and what can we expect in the years to come? Joining the conversation this time are: Joydeep Biswas (University of Texas at Austin), Sanmay Das (Virginia Tech), Rina Dechter (University of California, Irvine), Ioannis Erripis (AIhub), Sabine Hauert (University of Bristol), Ella Scallan (AIhub), and Marija Slavkovik (University of Bergen). Lucy Smith: There have been huge advancements in humanoid robots over the past couple of years. Today’s topic is particularly timely, as RoboCup 2026 recently took place. I thought it would be interesting to start with an overview of recent developments at RoboCup. Joydeep Biswas: This all started snowballing a couple of years ago, and we suddenly started to see this huge inflection on the capabilities. New humanoid robots were showing up at RoboCup that didn’t fall down as much. Suddenly we were able to deploy robots without humans following them around. I want to highlight that this is not just one key technical innovation, it required the confluence of a wide number of things: much better hardware, significant advances in algorithms, and advances in how we train and learn. Once upon a time, humanoid robots required classical control. However, most modern humanoid robots are using learned controllers for walking. So the rise of doing sim-to-real, like training these models in simulation and transferring them to the real world, are new algorithmic innovations. This year we had 55 humanoid robot soccer teams at the international competition, which is a lot for an international competition. We had a demo game of 11 vs 11 humanoid robots . Every year we have the RoboCup trustees play against the robots to see where we’re at. It used to be trivial. I won’t say it was hard this year, but I will say it’s getting less easy for the trustees as the years go by. RoboCup has recognized that we are at the inflection point, and at the trustees level we’ve been thinking about how to restructure our competitions to focus on these big advances coming up. We’ve simplified our soccer leagues significantly – in 2028, there will only be humanoid league soccer. Once upon a time, we couldn’t have a fully integrated humanoid robot capable of doing everything. Even though it’s not perfect today, we have the ability to integrate control, perception etc. We feel that from the scientific perspective, it is worth exploring having everything integrated into one robot form. Sabine Hauert: I started out excited about robotics because of RoboCup. I was in Manuela Veloso’s team doing the aibo (robot dogs) league. And that got me excited about robots working together. And then from there, they went on to the Nao robots and then to the humanoids. I guess this is a way to shake things up and to get it to the next level. Generally, I think the humanoid shift has been fascinating. And looking at ICRA and IROS , just the sheer shift in what’s on that exhibit floor over the years is really quite drastic. It used to be all drones and then it was all robot dogs and now it’s all hands and humanoids. There are also some of the more industrial robots that have been there for a while. But that shift is very striking because you walk around and there’s just so many of them. And at the robot parade you just see all these humanoid form factors and it’s very exciting from the hardware perspective. In addition there have been beautiful advances in the control to make that hardware and shape form work. I’m very excited for other robots, actually, not necessarily humanoids, because some of that technology can be transferred. I don’t know that we need humanoids for everything. I’m still very much in the category of people that think we need task-specific robots so that we can build them for the things that they’re meant to do. Maybe we get a general form factor not through having a human form, but by having lots of different robots with different form factors that work together, giving you the same capabilities as a human, but through multiplication rather than putting everything in one agent. But humanoids are part of the ecosystem, and I think they’re boosting the field, and so there’s a lot to gain from that. Ella Scallan: Are humanoids the most effective shape to get tasks done? Joydeep: No! The argument has been that everyday environments are designed for the human factor. So if you could have a working robot which has a humanoid factor, they could be a drop-in replacement and be able to use the tools and the environments which humans can. There is one big presupposition there: that we have functioning humanoid robots. As of today, that is absolutely not the case. In fact, if you want to have something work well today, there are very few cases where you could argue that the humanoid robot is the best solution. I think being a researcher in this area, it’s great to actually think a little bit about how we get to that eventual goal. Humanoids are rarely the correct solution for an application. Simple tasks, which are what we would call kinematic planning (for example, they are position-based – you want to pick up a block and put it somewhere else), are better with a wheeled robot, because the base is stable, and much easier with simpler planners, which have fewer degrees of freedom. You add a humanoid, suddenly the complexity increases. Now you’re not just worrying about position, you’re worrying about position and forces and velocities and accelerations which has much higher dimensions for planning. And it’s just not very easy to do. There are many more reasons too, that’s just one example. Marija Slavkovik: Can I give a historical anecdote here in response to that? A humanoid shape is not necessarily the best thing. Douglas Bader was a pilot in the Royal Air Force in the Second World War. He was considered to be a better pilot because he didn’t have legs, which he lost in an accident. And because he didn’t have legs, he was able to better handle high acceleration. There are some pretty horrible examples of children being used because their smaller bodies were better suited to the task, like kid jockeys on camels, children in mines, or in weaving. Of course, these are all examples of people, but their bodies are not what you think about when you say humanoid robot. Sanmay Das: I mean, it’s an interesting set of questions. I was wandering around one of these big conventions recently, and it was all about AI and robotics and very government tech/dev tech-focused. But one of the things they had that people were really interested in was this robot barista. You could ask it to make a coffee and it was going around doing things with the arms, but it wasn’t producing particularly good coffee from what I could tell. And I was thinking I have a semi-automatic espresso machine that I press a button on that does a really good job of making good coffee. I don’t see why we need this extremely complicated thing. But at the same time, people like it, right? How much of this is that people are more comfortable engaging with robots in this form? I think that one of the main things that we need to be careful about is anthropomorphization. I think for robotics, especially as they become more and more capable, this is really going to become a question. People will anthropomorphize these humanoid robots in ways that they will not your Roombas and your robot dogs and so on, and do we want that? And I think that that’s going to be an interesting question to think about. Ella: Even creating humanoid robots is an act of anthropromorphization.They aren’t the most effective shape for the task, so we’re sacrificing some function for form. Marija: Speaking of what we want, I’ve seen videos of robots that roll into a bathroom and clean it. They use the same brush for the toilet and the sink, but that’s a separate problem. My question is: how realistic are these? Because they’re just promotional videos: “invest now, and in one year, these are going to be real” . I even see some folding laundry, which is the holy grail, right? Robotics wise, are we there yet? Joydeep: I think you bring up an excellent point, which is truth in advertising. We are definitely seeing a lot of new capabilities that we didn’t have before, but we have to be honest about what they are and are not capable of. For many actors, it is in their best interests to promote the best of their platforms and hide the worst just because of the financial incentives. If you think a little bit about what went into setting up the demo, how many takes did it actually take you to do it? How over engineered was it for that very specific scenario? It worked with a particular brush, what if I gave it a slightly different brush? What if the light was turned off and it was on? And I can tell you the answer here is that none of these solutions are really robust. They’re definitely not general purpose. The best advancements are definitely over-optimized to very specific scenarios. Also the ways in which they’re being trained are just not scalable for doing the wider broad set of things that we want to do. So I think as a community, we need to demand and require truth in advertising. And the downside of this huge influx of companies in the space is that the incentives for scientific advancement are not necessarily well aligned with the advancement of companies today. Sabine: I think there’s a sense that people think it’s been done because they’ve seen it in a video, when a lot of it is either remote controlled or very fine-tuned for the scenarios that they’ve been designed for, as Joydeep mentions. There isn’t a “get your humanoid out-of-the-box and have it doing something useful in an environment it’s never seen before” because the data’s not there, it’s not been trained there. Joydeep: Yes. Even for a wheeled robot, we don’t have that capability. Rina Dechter: Thinking about one use case, robotics for social interaction with humans, for example if you wanted healthcare assistance or similar, psychologically it might give a better impression if you were assisted by a humanoid than a box. It may make a difference to people. But in other cases I agree, the best form for the robot depends on the tasks. Joydeep: I 100% agree. I think also it’s the challenge of the latest capabilities of our current research algorithms, because behind the capabilities that we’re seeing today are things like reinforcement learning and learning from demonstration. This is great for non-human interactive stuff like manipulating objects, but it doesn’t really scale well to human interaction. You can’t collect a very large number of demonstrations of a robot interacting with a person because there’s no one person. Everybody is different. And you can’t simulate a human realistically either. So the capabilities that we are using to bring these advances are just not very good for the human interaction capability that we need for the important problems. Sabine: At the Bristol Robotics Laboratory we have the assistive living research facility and there are all these robots that are beautiful for human-robot interaction. So probably there’s a nice space for the humanoid form in those caring settings as long as they’re not deceiving in the way that we worry about from an ethical perspective. You also expect more from your humanoid in terms of its capabilities somehow because of its human shape. So somehow the cartoony ones that weren’t that capable were maybe better for those settings, also safer. I’ve seen so many videos of these humanoids toppling over in crowds. Rina: What I found really impressive was when robots started to talk using LLMs. It really was amazing. And this is because it’s more going towards the human. It has moved from just writing text to generating it and voicing it. I think it’s easier to be influenced and believe something that’s a human-like object. Marija: I wonder how much of this humanoid obsession comes from science fiction’s original picturing of humanoid robots? That sets the shape of the robot and the term robot. So everything is already pre-biased to be in that shape. It makes for a better story. Whereas if it is some kind of a box that does something, you have to do a lot of explaining as to what the robot is and what it does. I remember watching the Roomba clean the floor for the first time, and it was a very annoying experience because it’s not doing the things the way you would have done them. Sabine: Also, because AI has had such advances with LLMs, I think people just see humanoids as the next obvious thing that will definitely happen. This is now seen as the normal form factor for a more general form of intelligence. And so there’s this obviousness to it. In some discussions, people have really been pushing me for an answer on when humanoids are going to work the way we expect. And I don’t know. RoboCup has an answer for that, right, because they have an aim to get them playing at human level against the trustees. Joydeep: Well, I won’t say Robocup has an answer. Robocup has a challenge to defeat the human world champions by 2050. That’s more an open conjecture. You raised an important point that not everybody in the general public is aware of. There’s an equivocation of the capabilities needed. People see the capabilities of chatbots and you think that a robot picking up a laptop is trivial. But that’s because they’re equivocating what is hard as a human to what is hard for a robot, but it’s absolutely not true. In fact, doing the so-called very high-level planning in some sense can be easier for a robot than interacting with the embodied world. This is Moravec’s paradox. Lots of roboticists have spoken about this, but I think there’s a gap in the public perception of what is easy versus hard and the disconnect between what is easy and hard for a human versus what’s easy and hard for a robot. Sabine: And there’s also just the data. We had buckets of data for language that we don’t have in the physical world. Joydeep: We don’t have the internet of physical interactions. Marija: Well, we now have people being paid to do manual movements that are supposed to be somehow used for training afterwards. Joydeep: Yeah, so there’s a huge effort right now across so many companies spending so many millions to billions of dollars on what’s called teleoperation. And that is a human controlling a robot to do a task because that data can be used to train a robot. And yes, it is true, it is useful data, but there’s a divide even in the robotics community. There are some people who believe this is all you need – you just need to scale up. There are other people, like me, who don’t buy the argument that more teleoperation data is going to get us to general purpose robots. And I think the reason for that is rather simple. It’s that the complexity of the tasks that we want to do has combinatorial explosion. And we’re never going to have that level of demonstrations. And the other thing here is that we’ve seen this craze before with self-driving cars. If you think back, in 2014, maybe a little bit earlier, a common narrative among self-driving companies was that we just needed to go out and build HD maps of our environment and that’s all we needed. Like driving would be solved. Guess what? It didn’t turn out to be the case. This current craze about collecting data and mimicking humans feels very similar to that era. That’s not to say it wasn’t useful. But I don’t think that alone is going to solve the problem. Marija: I agree with you as a non-expert in this, because humans do things the way humans do them, and machines do them the way machines do them. Birds fly, airplanes fly, but not in the same way. Again, with my non-able body examples, people without legs don’t “walk” like people with legs, right? Sabine: One reason the humanoid form might make a lot of sense in robotics from the data perspective is human video. There’s loads of human video. And I’m guessing the reason for that is they collect the data from the humans rather than have them teleoperate a robotic system. And then things need to have a similar physical frame for those videos of humans then to translate to the capabilities of the robots. We recently did tests with VLMs [vision-language models] and it was harder to use that data that’s already available in these trained models because data is human-centric, and our robots are not in humanoid form. Joydeep: I think what you said is absolutely true. We have a ton of videos on YouTube of humans doing tasks. The mismatch of course is the data; the way that data was collected was using very different sensors than what robots would have. So there is a mismatch there beyond the mismatch of the embodiment. But many of us agree that that data is useful. Ella: If the solution to get general purpose robots isn’t more data, do we need to wait for better AI and better learning methods? Joydeep: All the time. I mean, there’s one thing that’s clear. I think many of us believe that experience from interaction is crucial. You don’t learn just by mimicking what someone else did. You learn by getting some initial understanding based on seeing what other people did, but then trying it out and gaining intuition. And this is true for learning algorithms as well. If the expert shows you how to do a thing, and if you can do exactly what the expert did, you’ll be good. But invariably what happens is that if you try to do exactly what the expert did, you make one mistake and suddenly you’re in a state which you did not have in the expert demonstration. Now what do you do? You don’t have any training data for that, right? So this is why experience is useful and important. Rina: From a causality perspective, the language we use is that there is observational data and interventional data. Causality cannot be gleaned just from observation, you have to interact in order to see what’s going on. Joydeep: Yeah. I think interaction is the best way to exploit some of the behaviors that Marija was talking about, like getting behaviors optimized to the form and functionality that you have. Sabine: I do worry though about this idea that now we need better robots or better AI to complete useful tasks. We were so close to getting our robots that were simple working really well, with enough computation on board, good sensing, that they were useful in lots of different ways. And now somehow we’ve moved the goalposts towards robots that are maybe not as green, not as easy to verify and test etc because they’re in a more complex form factor. And so I worry that we’re going to keep moving the goalposts instead of benefiting from all the stuff that already works in the robotics field and trying to get that out into applications. And the fundraising kind of shows that: the humanoids are raising and it’s harder to raise if you’re not in this next wave of humanoids or physical AI. We need to make sure it doesn’t end up being the only way forward. Joydeep: In a talk I give I have a slide about this. I talk about the open challenges for robots and say that you need the following to have a successful mobile robot: a sufficiently detailed map of the world, an accurate predefined notion of action costs, a well-defined task objective, a curated list of entities of interest, no surprises, and enough onboard sensing and compute. This is a very large caveat list, but in settings such as manufacturing and logistics, these can all be achieved. But the moment you take any of these caveats out, suddenly you’re in the research landscape. And that’s kind of where we’re at. Sabine: The other thing I heard is that people are calling everything humanoids, so the word has taken over. It’s got a lot of excitement, it’s helping to raise funds. And then you’ll have a wheeled humanoid, or a humanoid with six arms, for example. And there will all be forms of humanoids. So it’ll go full circle back to the different form factors. Marija: If you think about it, a computer playing chess does little for solving general AI tasks. But it acted as a catalyst to attract attention, funding and resources so that they can be used to actually develop deep learning and so on. So maybe it works out in the end. You create this magic for people to believe in and invest in, and something else comes out of it. Although I’m not going to say I’m advocating this, it’s definitely borderline fraud sometimes, these videos of depicted abilities. It’s just easier to sell, right? That was the trick, Sabine, that whenever somebody asks you when we are going to see useful or capable humanoids, you can ask them what they mean by useful or capable. Because then you turn around the question. People understand that we already have very many useful and capable things. Sabine: Yeah, so they were asking when the breakthrough was going to be. I say the breakthrough is when we see all those robots that work in everyday environments, not necessarily humanoid, and all the things we’re pushing research-wise out in the world. And I think that’s the breakthrough. Joydeep: I think even before ChatGPT was released December 2022, and folks who were playing with these large language models, GPT 2, 3, etc, we were seeing capabilities which were very hard to do beforehand. What really made it break through in the public consciousness was having a public-facing website – that was an inflection point. I doubt that for the robotic space we’re going to see a similar inflection point where suddenly we’re able to see generational new capabilities. I think we’re probably going to see slow adoption of robots in limited capabilities and specific scenarios, increasingly more and more and more. It’s just going to be a very slow adoption. We’re not going to suddenly have a robot capable of doing it all. Marija: If any of you see a robot that folds laundry or irons laundry, wake me up in the middle of the night. To me, that’s the breakthrough point. If I see one of them, I don’t care how much it costs. Joydeep: Well, again, the question is, under what conditions? If you are okay with a few hours to fold your laundry and specific kinds of laundry. Marija: It can take as much time as it wants, let’s make it one week maximum. But no caveats. You have to take it out of the dryer and fold it in a neat stack, unspecified laundry. I mean, think about it. Would you care how long it takes as long as it’s done? How long does it take me, the lazy human to do it? Three days it’s going to live in the dryer until I get to it. Joydeep: Yeah, so the challenges here are robustness. So you said it should not matter what the laundry is, and you want a certain degree of accuracy. You don’t want that every fifth attempt, it makes a catastrophic failure, and then you have to go rescue the robot. Now, not only do you have to do your laundry on your own, you also have to rescue the robot. I think as humans we have very high expectations for autonomy, which we don’t explicitly mention, which is fine, but I think that’s the challenge. In research papers, we say that an 80% success rate is phenomenal. No, 80% success rate as a product is awful. It’s a failure. Or even 99%, it’s still not good enough. Ioannis Erripis: I have two small questions. Firstly, I’ve seen recently at least three companies that are advertising household humanoid robots. What do you think about those? Sabine: The remote controlled ones. Joydeep: Yeah, there’s certainly not anything which can do all household tasks autonomously. They’re actually using you for data collection. Sabine: There’s a company in San Francisco that will pay you to do your household cleaning, because they collect data from your house. Ioannis: My second question is more maybe superficial. What do you think about the design of most of the humanoid robots? And let me rephrase this a bit more specifically. One of my favourite robots was maybe Honda’s ASIMO, which looked like an astronaut toy. If you see behind the glass, it is smiling and has a very cute face. It’s a robot that you would easily give as a gift to your child, for example. But almost all humanoid robots are very menacing. They almost look like a villain from a movie. And actually, at the same time, they aspire to be adopted by consumers. What do you think about this? To me, it looks like a very unorthodox approach. Joydeep: I think you’re absolutely right, but there are companies which are trying to build humanoid robots which are human approachable. Fauna Robotics is one of them. They are very much leaning into exactly what you’re saying. Ioannis: I guess that’s an exception. Joydeep: I agree it’s an exception, and I think partly that is because the capabilities that we’re really missing today are these fine-grained motor skills. People are trying to think about whether we can just build a form and understand how we can solve these fine-grained motor skills, and then we’ll talk about the interaction. But you’re absolutely right that we should think about them jointly.

items.content: Digit 5 includes redesigned legs and new batteries for commercial use. Source: Agility Robotics Agility Robotics has cleared a major hurdle in its planned initial public offering (IPO). Shareholders of Churchill Capital Corp XI approved the special purpose acquisition company’s (SPAC) proposed business combination with the humanoid developer, moving Agility closer to becoming a publicly-traded company. More than 84% of votes cast at a special shareholder meeting on Nov. 2 supported the deal. The SPAC is expected to close on Nov. 4. The combined company is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Nov. 5 under the ticker symbol AGLT. Churchill Capital stock finished up nearly 14% on Nov. 2.  The transaction is expected to provide Agility with approximately $465 million in gross capital before expenses. That funding will support commercial expansion, customer deployments and manufacturing capacity as the company looks to scale its Digit humanoid robot business. The revised capital figure reflects a reduction from the more than $620 million in gross proceeds anticipated when the merger was announced in June. Following the expiration of Churchill XI’s shareholder redemption deadline, the companies now expect approximately $164 million from Churchill’s trust account, approximately $201 million from a private investment in public equity (PIPE) financing led by Foxconn, and $100 million in equity funding Agility received following the initial SPAC announcement. The original transaction valued Agility at a $2.5 billion pre-money equity value. Existing Agility shareholders will roll their equity into the combined company rather than receive cash in the transaction. Agility is entering the public markets with more than a proposed product roadmap. Its Digit robots are already operating in 9 customer environments, with logistics and manufacturing emerging as the company’s primary commercial markets. One of its most established relationships is with GXO Logistics. The companies began working together in 2023 and signed a multi-year Robots-as-a-Service agreement in 2024 to deploy Digit at GXO’s facility in Flowery Branch, Ga. There, Digit has worked alongside existing automation to move totes and place them onto conveyors. In October, the companies announced an expansion to two additional GXO facilities: Statesville, N.C., and Lebanon, Tenn. Digit will initially support repetitive material-handling tasks in e-commerce fulfillment operations. Deployments are expected to begin in early 2027 using Digit 4, with plans to transition to the newer Digit 5 as it becomes commercially available. Agility is also moving into manufacturing. In October, agricultural equipment maker AGCO signed a commercial agreement to pilot Digit at its Hesston , Kan., production facility beginning in 2027. Initial tasks will include sorting and stacking parts and placing totes for storage. Submit your innovation now! Agility has previously claimed it has more than $300 million in committed multi-year orders for Digit 5 , its next-generation humanoid unveiled in September. The company says early access for customers is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability targeted for the end of that year. That order figure is an important indicator of customer interest, but it should not be confused with current revenue. The multi-year value is expected to be realized over time and remains subject to contractual milestones, product features and specifications. Agility’s RoboFab manufacturing facility in Salem, Ore., is designed for annual production capacity of up to 10,000 robots. The company is also expanding its software, deployment and service capabilities, including through its Agility Arc fleet-management platform. Agility Robotics co-founder and chief robot officer Jonathan Hurst (right) during the opening keynote at RoboBusiness 2026 with (left to right) Steve Crowe (The Robot Report), Rodney Brooks (Robust AI) and Ken Goldberg (UC Berkeley). items.content: October 2026 was a whirlwind month for the robotics industry. Last month, we celebrated the 20th anniversary of RoboBusiness and announced that next year, the show will be rebranded to Robotics Summit & Expo West. In addition, prominent humanoid robot companies, such as Agility Robotics and Boston Dynamics, announced some major updates. Here are the 10 most popular articles on The Robot Report in the past month. Subscribe to The Robot Report newsletter and listen to The Robot Report Podcast to stay up to date on the latest robotics news. 10. AGCO to deploy Agility Digit humanoid in Kansas factory In October 2026, AGCO and Agility Robotics signed a commercial agreement to deploy Agility’s Digit humanoid in AGCO’s manufacturing facility. The U.S. pilot, expected to begin in 2027, will support AGCO’s efforts to create more flexible, intelligent factories, beginning at its site in Hesston, Kan. Read more . 9. Will ‘boring’ robots win in the real world? Why robotic form should follow workflow Robots have captured our imagination. We have seen humanoids balancing on one leg, doing backflips, folding laundry, and moving smoothly over difficult terrain. This is all behavior that only a few years ago seemed like something out of science fiction. These viral examples matter because they show that embodied AI has reached a new technical stage. Read more . 8. Agility and GXO Logistics plan expanded deployment of Digit humanoid Agility Robotics and GXO Logistics said they are expanding their partnership to deploy the Digit humanoid robot in GXO sites in North Carolina and Tennessee. Read more . 7. Boston Dynamics gives more insight into its redesigned humanoid hand Boston Dynamics in October 2026 gave a look at its new humanoid hand. The four-fingered gripper has 13 degrees of freedom, or DoF, and is directly actuated. The company said it designed it for mass production. Read more . 6. Promise Robotics partners with D.R. Horton on physical AI for homebuilding in October 2026 The construction industry is fragmented and has been relatively conservative about adopting new technologies, but physical AI promises to modernize homebuilding. Promise Robotics said it has signed a multi-year agreement with D.R. Horton, which will use its Factory-as-a-Service capabilities to produce more than 1,250 homes in the U.S. Read more . 5. AWS launches open-source Physical AI Toolchain for robotics Amazon Web Services launched an open-source Physical AI Toolchain designed to help roboticists move from collecting data to training, simulating, validating and deploying AI models on their robots. The toolchain brings together AWS services and NVIDIA’s Physical AI software stack into a single development workflow. Read more . 4. Previous versions of Atlas’ hand featured seven degrees of freedom and were designed to grasp a large variety of objects, Boston Dynamics said. With the latest hand, the company is shifting its focus to manipulating those objects. Read more . 2. The company has named Rohit Prasad as its new CEO. Prasad will take over from Chief Financial Officer Amanda McMaster, who served as interim CEO. Read more . 1. items.content: Robotics companies are investing heavily in the belief that data will solve the most difficult problems in robotics. Once AI systems have ingested enough data from human demonstrations, the thinking goes, robots will be able to perform the vast majority of the manual tasks that humans now do. There are even robotics companies that exist solely to collect training data and sell it to other robotics companies in pursuit of this goal. But whether data will finally bring us general-purpose robots is an open question . Nobody knows how much data would be necessary , what kind of data is important , or whether something else might be missing . And there are other problems with a reliance on massive amounts of data: the resulting AI algorithms are essentially black boxes, which despite their high performance are difficult or impossible for humans to understand. This characteristic is becoming increasingly concerning in commercial deployments, where robots must be flexible, reliable, and safe. At the 2026 Conference on Robot Learning this week, UC Berkeley and NVIDIA are jointly announcing a new approach to using AI to program robots for everyday practical tasks in industrial environments. Called agentic robotics, this technique leverages the latest advances in AI coding tools while in some sense bringing robotics back to its roots—achieving a fundamental understanding of how a robot works, and then writing human-readable code to get it to do useful things, no data (and no humans) required. The Data Problem For decades, robots were programmed with model-based methods, meaning that their behavior was based on a detailed understanding (or model) of the physics and mathematics underlying the robot and its environment. Roboticists would first develop these models, and then write painstakingly detailed code telling their robots how to act. The resulting hand-tuned robotic systems could operate fast and reliably, but this approach has fallen out of favor because it requires both human time and human expertise. It’s much easier to just feed a huge amount of human demonstration data into a machine-learning system, and the results that come out are both adaptable and reliable—up to a point. “The imitation learning paradigm has hit a plateau,” explains Ken Goldberg , a professor of robotics at UC Berkeley whose lab is presenting a paper on agentic robotics at this week’s conference. “It’s promising for things like home robots, where speed and reliability are less of an issue. But for industrial applications, it’s very hard to get the reliability that industry requires.” Goldberg, who is also a co-founder of the industrial robotics company Ambi Robotics , has experienced this problem firsthand, as have other companies that he’s been working with, including Siemens and Bosch. “You get good performance from data initially, but then things go wrong. So you start giving it more data. But then other things go wrong. It’s not clear that adding more data is going to get you there.” The hope, according to Goldberg, is that with enough data, robots will somehow just start to work reliably, since that was the case with ChatGPT. “That’s what people have been counting on, and why investors are pouring money into these companies,” says Goldberg. “But everybody’s getting a little nervous that we haven’t hit that convergence point.” How Agentic Robotics Works The reason why language models like ChatGPT are so successful is that they can train on data at the scale of the Internet. There is no dataset for robotics that approaches that scale, and while robotics companies are desperately attempting to generate the data that they think they need, it’s a slow, expensive process. Agentic robotics, a term popularized by Goldberg along with Spencer Huang , Director of Product for Robotics at NVIDIA, is an attempt to turn programming robots from a data problem into a coding problem, which can directly leverage the scale of language models. “This is really something that’s accelerated in the past year,” Goldberg says. “The quality of agentic coding has become so good that using them to write code for robots is now viable.” Because agentic robotics is based on LLMs, it’s easy to use—you can use natural language to tell the robot what to do. One example used by the UC Berkeley researchers was asking a robotic arm to pack groceries into a bag. First, this relatively complex (to a robot) task is decomposed into simpler sub-tasks, each of them assigned to a separate coding agent. In LLM-based software, a coding agent is an autonomous AI system that can plan, write, test, and modify software with minimal human intervention. You might have one individual agent tasked with perception to identify the groceries and the bag, a second focused on object manipulation with the arm’s gripper, and a third working on transporting objects with the arm once they’ve been grasped. “We have all these robotics tools we’ve been building for the last couple decades,” explains Huang. “The problem was that a human had to go and write the code themselves. But object classifiers, pose estimation, task and motion planning, trajectory generation—everything is already there.” The coding agents can directly leverage all of that existing data contained within their language models to generate code of their own, tailored to their specific tasks. Solving the Simulation Bottleneck Once the agents have a plausible framework, they run their code in a simulation and see what happens, much like a human would. They can change starting conditions, identify failures, refine the code, and keep iterating until they’ve got a successful program. Of course, code that works in simulation can only ever be as versatile and reliable as the simulation is. “Simulations are non-trivial to build,” Goldberg explains. The more accurate the simulation has the potential to be, the more parameters there are that need to be configured to achieve and maintain that accuracy, typically by a human on a task-by-task basis. Goldberg decided to try giving an AI agent direct access to these simulation parameters, and instructing it to match the simulation to a video of the real world. “It gave us goosebumps. It was matching the whole environment, the lighting, the background, all these things that are super tedious to do. We would never have done that, but the agent did. Side by side, it was very hard to tell the difference between the simulation and the video.” Nevertheless, no matter how good a simulated environment looks, navigating the gap between that environment and the real world is still an unsolved challenge for the robotics community, says Torsten Kroeger , chief science officer at Alphabet’s Intrinsic . Kroeger, who is not directly involved in this research, continued: “I’m saying this respectfully, but there’s just no physics engine out there that can accurately model physical contact with the world.” But as with a team of human coders, the agents can troubleshoot when things inevitably don’t work quite right. The agents’ ability to work on the simulation itself offers significant advantages, because the agents can be fed video of a failed task with the goal of updating the simulation to match, while the coding agents then iterate to fix the problem. As with anything done by AI, Huang is well aware that agents writing code for robots will have their flaws. “We all know that AI agents can create slop,” Huang says. “In order to counter that, we use adversarial agent setups—where one agent designs something and another agent tries to rip it apart and find flaws.” In UC Berkeley’s testing , agentic robotics approaches were able to reach success rates of up to 99 percent, matching human hand-engineered performance, even in tasks where baseline imitation learning techniques saw success rates of only 20 percent. But as Goldberg points out, agentic robotics is not just about performance, but also about efficiency and safety. “You’re using an off the shelf coding agent. You don’t need to collect any data. And the agent is generating code that you can actually understand and fix if necessary.” Real World Agentic Robotics In the immediate future, the sweet spot for practical agentic robotics will be industrial manufacturing and manipulation tasks that require robust precision and accuracy , says Huang. “Right now, some of our partners in the semiconductor space need to place components within 0.3 mm. There’s no way you’re going to get something like GR00T [NVIDIA’s humanoid development platform] to do that today with any semblance of repeatability and robustness. What you get with agentic robotics is near-term applications.” But the real value, Huang says, is in adapting to change. “At Wistron in Taiwan [which manufactures baseboards for NVIDIA GPUs], every time they add a new product, it takes a minimum of 8 hours to retask one robot. With agentic robotics, retasking takes a minute or two instead.” Moving agentic robotics beyond these fairly well-constrained use cases may be difficult, but Huang sees this technique as a gateway towards more complex tasks. “Agentic robotics can generate tons of good quality robotic code, which is data that we can use for training the next model.” Such code generation is only an iterative step towards a general purpose capability, but Huang believes that agentic robotics may help redefine the very meaning of general intelligence in the context of robotics. “My thesis is that general intelligence for robotics will first come in the form of an agent orchestrating a mix of conventional technologies and specialized policies. To a human, it looks like general intelligence because the agent is coordinating everything under the hood.” Intrinsic’s Kroeger is more cautious about placing trust in agents. “In the context of safety and security, how do we know that these agents are really doing the right thing all the time? It’s the alignment problem . A human engineer can review everything, but the challenge will be once we start putting our trust in these agents. I can imagine that this will become a relevant conversation for the industry.” For now, Goldberg is focused on working with real companies to put agentic robotics into practice. A series of benchmarks for agentic robotics developed with NVIDIA Isaac Lab-Arena and the Newton physics engine will help researchers evaluate agent performance. “I don’t want to say that we have the solution, but I’m very excited about it,” he says. Adds Huang: “It’s a pivotal change in the way we’re doing things.”

[ HEBI ] Something strange has been happening at KIMLAB. Our snacks kept disappearing… and we finally caught the culprit. Meet GG, our new lab friend. GG is a character robot inspired by the Ggeomeoksali from Netflix’s “The East Palace.” GG sneaks around for snacks, eats them, sleeps most of the time, begs everyone for more food, and leans on whoever is nearby. Cute, comforting, and a good friend. But GG is still a gwi-mae… so who knows what else it can do. [ Kinetic Intelligent Machine Lab ] Happy Halloween from Dusty Robotics! [ Dusty ] Finally, a robot with a butt. [ JSK Lab ] Thanks, Shunnosuke! Any drone can crash into a tree once. This drone can crash into a tree MORE than once. [ ETH Zurich ] Lume is a robotic floor lamp that moves around your home, helps with everyday chores, and returns to being a beautiful lamp when it’s done. [ Syncere ] If we’re going to use robots at work or at home, they’re going to have to communicate with us. At Toyota Research Institute, a team of robotics user experience designers is working on the sounds, gestures, light patterns, and interfaces that allow robots to let us know that they are on the move, that we need to stay clear, or to tell us that they just really need help. Steffi Paepcke, Director of Robotics User Experience at TRI, accepts the challenge to explain how her team approaches this work in just one minute. I need a sound for when people around me need to give me space. [ Toyota Research Institute ] The entirely student-run, self-taught and highly collaborative MIT Combat Robotics Club (CRC) builds high-energy fighting machines to compete in House Battles and larger competitions. Fans of the hit show BattleBots may remember some of CRC’s past robots, including Uppercut, SawBlaze, the Dentist, and Overhaul. CRC is open to every MIT student regardless of year, major, or prior experience. Students learn a variety of skills, from CAD and FEA to CNC Machining and Welding—and they learn through watching their creations get completely destroyed. [ MIT Combat Robotics Club ] Happy birthday, JPL ! Where do I get a shirt like that last guy has? [ JPL ] Can machines be creative? In this first episode of Moonshot, host Mike Massimino talks with Hod Lipson, a Columbia Engineering roboticist whose work includes robots that learn and adapt. Lipson, the James and Sally Scapa Professor of Innovation in Columbia’s Department of Mechanical Engineering, explains why physical AI is so difficult, how engineers and AI might work together on new designs, and how he defines creativity. He also shares advice on why playing it safe can limit your impact. [ Columbia University ] This closing fireside chat brings together two of the field’s most consequential builders—Jeff Dean, whose work at Google has helped define the modern AI stack, and Fei-Fei Li, whose case for human-centered AI has shaped how the field thinks about who this technology should actually serve. Coming at the end of a day spent grappling with AI’s risks and unresolved questions, the conversation turns to where the two of them agree, where they don’t, and what they think the choices ahead really come down to. items.content: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) reconstructs a flow field from the motion of tracer particles but the reconstruction quality is bounded by how well the flow structure of interest is resolved in the images. The acquisition position is typically fixed by the operator before the measurement. We cast camera placement as a sequential decision-making problem and train a reinforcement learning agent to control a 6-DoF manipulator equipped with a camera, enabling it to locate, frame and resolve a hydrofoil wake in a water tunnel. The agent commands the camera pose and observes the scene only through the velocity field and uncertainty estimated from time-separated image pairs. It is trained entirely in a photorealistic simulation of our water tunnel, with wakes generated by Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations of hydrofoils with varying profiles, positions and angles of attack. After zero-shot transfer to the real water tunnel, the policy reliably locates and frames the wakes of randomly placed hydrofoils. It resolves the wake at a higher resolution than a fixed camera view and with lower error in the measured flow statistics, in roughly half the time of a full scan and with far fewer image pairs.

items.content: The Robot Report Podcast · What AgTech founders get wrong about ROI Connie Bowen, founding general partner of Farmhand Ventures. In Episode 268 of The Robot Report Podcast, our guest is Connie Bowen, the founding general partner of Farmhand Ventures, a venture fund with a focus on AgTech investments. Farmhand Ventures is an impact-first investment firm shaping the future of work in agriculture . It enables strategic programs and innovation to make farm work more attractive, productive, profitable, and resilient — improving the lives and livelihoods of farmers, farmworkers, and rural communities. A lifelong ag leader and engineer, Bowen has planted orchards, harvested hemp, and managed farm crews. That experience grounds her investment lens in the realities of the field. Over the past decade, Bowen has built a career connecting agricultural technology with practical farming needs, holding roles at The Yield Lab, AgLaunch, Chess Ag Full Harvest Partners, and Grape Arbor Ventures before founding Farmhand. Connie has backed dozens of agtech startups aligned with Farmhand’s mission — including L5 Automation, Scout, New West Genetics, and Nutt Bio. items.title: Show HN: DBDelve – Open-Source DB Client Made with Rust and GPUI
items.summary:
Hi HN, I’m Shayan and a few months ago I started building a DB Client DBDelve with a focus on performance and just making something that feels good to use (in the spirit of Zed, Ghostty, and other tools that just feel pleasant to use).

For my workflow I’ve always looked for performance, especially since some time ago I had a really outdated machine and any kind of bloat was really noticeable, I remember using DBeaver and it just crashing on me multiple times, I also had to use postGIS which just made it worse. I migrated all my essential dev tools to use the ones with performance in mind (Zed, Ghostty etc) but the only thing that was missing was DB Client. The main choices everyone has are DBeaver which is a memory hog and an overkill for most of the tasks imo. The other options like Datagrid, Beekeeper, TablePlus are either electron based so bloated and memory hogs or paid and closed-source.

DBDelve 0.3.6 against DBeaver 25.3.1 on the same Postgres table, median of 5 runs each (2026-10-11, M1 Pro, 32 GB). Times are from the action to the rows rendered.

                            DBDelve   DBeaver
  Launch                    1.1 s     5.2 s
  Idle memory               133 MB    606 MB
  1,000-row query           0.21 s    1.96 s
  1M rows, time             56 s      208 s
  1M rows, memory [1]       4.9 GB    17 GB
[1] The whole 1M-row, 100-column table pulled into memory on purpose, with the row limit off. Not a normal use case; DBeaver's heap limit had to be raised manually for the benchmark.

Scrolling perf with 1 million rows loaded with 100 columns each: https://youtu.be/V2MOhJYFqIE

It has most of the features most devs would need for 90% of their workflow plus some more I thought would be a nice touch: Readonly, read-write and Full Access modes Glass themes (If you’re into them, I am) Keyboard focused with every keybinding customizable Organization of connections into projects

Me and some other folks have been daily driving it for more than a month now and most good feedback comes on it having a really simple UI to navigate, very stable for its age and the performance of course. I’m also sharing here because those people tell me this has potential to grow so I’m trying my hand at distributing it.

Just want to give a huge shoutout here to the Zed team for GPUI, it's a breeze to work with if you just get through them not updating the crate officially on crates.io but the community has found the solutions for it, you just have to dig deep for it. It performs extremely well and just the HTML-like structure of it, makes it easy to understand for someone from a web dev background and agents are very good at writing it too. GPUI component also solves a lot of problems with having a good component library we can use. I think for anyone starting a GPUI project now, GPUI-kit makes a lot of sense, it just bundles GPUI, GPUI-component together and has some optimizations adding retained mode which is experimental but could provide a lot of benefit, so think all things considered it should be the default way.

The major optimization I did was just lowering the memory overhead by using packed rows which reduced the memory usage by 40% on large datasets (8.1GB to 4.9GB on a 4GB table loaded in app), everything else came bundled in with Rust and GPUI mostly or they just made it very easy.

Limitations: It's not signed and notarized, identity verification from apple's side has been a nightmare but it should be signed soon. Don’t expect feature parity with more mature clients for now, the general direction of this right now is the zed way of adding features in but after making sure the core workflows are done with a high quality.

Do give it a try, you can import your connections from dbeaver and tableplus.

items.content: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.
